headline: Kirei is ultimately from written Chinese 綺麗, first attested in Japanese in the 1200s.

sources.quote: Ultimately from written Chinese 綺麗, 奇麗 /绮丽, 奇丽. First attested in Japanese in the 1200s.

headline: Amerika is from English America, a Latinization of the given name of Amerigo Vespucci (1451-1512).

sources.quote: Borrowed from English America, from New Latin America, feminine form of Americus, a Latinization of the given name of Amerigo Vespucci (1451-1512), an Italian explorer.

sources.quote: 御(お) (o-, honorific prefix) + 巡(まわ)り (mawari, “going around”, honorific suffix) + さん (-san)

sources.quote: 図(ず) (zu, “diagram”) + 表(ひょう) (hyō, “table”)

headline: Ichi, “market”, is found in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 市 (ichi). Found in the Kojiki of 712 CE.

headline: Ne originally meant a sound or cry made by an insect, bird or beast, and is first attested in the Kojiki of 712.

sources.quote: ⟨ne₂⟩ → */nəɨ/ → /ne/
From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712, with the phonetic spelling 泥.

The original meaning appears to have been "a sound or cry, as made by an insect, bird, or beast", likely related to the verb for making such a sound, 鳴く (naku, “to make a sound; to cry out”), as well as its doublet 泣く (naku, “to cry, to weep”). It is also likely related to 鳴る (naru, “to sound; to ring”).

headline: Akai is from the Early Middle Japanese adjective 赤し (akashi), cognate with 明るい (akarui, “bright”).

sources.quote: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 赤(あか)し (akashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). Cognate with 明るい (akarui, “bright”).

Medial voiceless plosives, like /-k-/, underwent voicing, then spirantization, then gliding, then being dropped, before /-i, -u, -e, -o/. As this intervocalic sound-change did not occur before /-a/(Hamano, 2000), Middle Japanese /akaki/ became /akai/ 赤い.
⟨akaki₁⟩ → */akakʲi/ → */akaɡʲi/ → */akaɣi/ → */akaji/ → */akai/.

headline: Kata's noun senses are attested from the 8th century, with suffix use later.

sources.quote: Noun senses are attested from the 8th century, with suffix use later. See 形(かた) (kata). Compare also 姿(すがた) (sugata, “appearance, likeness”), 模(かたぎ) (katagi, “model, pattern, template”).

headline: Geki, “drama”, is from Middle Chinese 劇.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 劇 /剧.

headline: Ayashii is the interjection あや (aya, “oh”) plus -shii.

sources.quote: From interjection あや (aya, “oh”) + しい (-shii).

headline: Wa, “ring”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wa.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *wa.

headline: Uramu was previously an upper bigrade verb, then became quadrigrade by the Edo period.

sources.quote: Previously declined as an upper bigrade verb, but then became quadrigrade by the Edo period, where it would also rarely conjugate as a monograde verb.

headline: Kizu's apparent relation to 切る (kiru, “to cut”) is rejected by the mid-vowel preservation in its Ryukyuan cognates.

sources.quote: ⟨ki₁zu⟩ → */kizu/ → /kizu/
From Old Japanese 瑕 (ki₁zu).
Any apparent relation to verb 切(き)る (kiru, “to cut”) is rejected by mid-vowel preservation of its Ryukyuan cognates.

headline: Yō, “way”, is from Middle Chinese 樣 (MC yangH).

sources.quote: /jɨau/ → /jɔː/ → /joː/
From Middle Chinese 樣 (MC yangH).

headline: Tsukare is the continuative form of 疲れる (tsukareru).

sources.quote: From the continuative form of 疲れる (tsukareru).

meaning: to do, to try; to wear small items (e.g., necktie, watch, etc.)
headline: Suru is from the Old Japanese verb す (su, “to do”), from Proto-Japonic *su, and cognate with Okinawan sun.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese verb す (su, “to do”), from Proto-Japonic *su. Cognate with Okinawan すん (sun).

As with all verbs, during the Middle Japanese stage in the Kamakura and Muromachi periods, the 終止形 (shūshikei, “terminal or sentence-ending form”) was gradually lost as the 連体形 (rentaikei, “attributive form”) came to be used for both the attributive and terminal grammatical roles, realigning the conjugations.

headline: Tsuma, “wife”, is from 端 (tsuma, “side, edge”): the person at someone's side, compare English better half.

sources.quote: From 端 (tsuma, “side, edge”), indicating the person who is at the side of someone: a spouse. Compare the English expression better half.
This term originally referred to either a male (husband) or female (wife) spouse. In modern usage, this term refers only to a female spouse.
By extension from the at the side sense.

headline: Miryoku is a wasei kango, first attested in 1911 in Jun'ichirō Tanizaki's short story 秘密 (Himitsu, “The Secret”).

sources.quote: Wasei kango from elements 魅(み) (mi, “charm, allure, fascination”) + 力(りょく) (-ryoku, “power”).
First attested in 1911 in Jun'ichirō Tanizaki's short story 秘密(ひみつ) (Himitsu, “The Secret”) (see quotation).

headline: Daigakuin is 大学 (daigaku) plus 院 (-in).

sources.quote: 大学(だいがく) (daigaku) + 院(いん) (-in)

headline: Saku, “plan”, is from Middle Chinese 策.

sources.quote: From Middle Chinese 策 (tsrheak).

meaning: to entrust to another, to leave to
headline: Makaseru is from Old Japanese 任す (makasu).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 任す (makasu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

meaning: to stop, to halt, to stand still
headline: Tachidomaru is 立つ (tatsu, “to stand”) plus 止まる (tomaru, “to stop”).

sources.quote: 立(た)つ (tatsu, “to stand”) + 止(と)まる (tomaru, “to stop”)

headline: Akubi is first attested in the Shinsen Jikyō of 898–901 CE, perhaps as the stem of the verb あくぶ (akubu).

sources.quote: Possibly from Old Japanese; first attested in the 新撰字鏡 (Shinsen Jikyō, “Newly Compiled Mirror of Characters”) of 898­­­–901 CE.

Appears to be derived as the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb あくぶ (akubu), although this verb form isn't attested until the 枕草子 (Makura Sōshi, “The Pillow Book”) of 1002.

headline: Oshie is the continuative stem of 教える (oshieru).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 教(おし)える (oshieru).

headline: Sabi, “rust”, is the continuative stem of 錆びる (sabiru, “to rust”).

sources.quote: From 錆び (sabi), the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 錆(さ)びる (sabiru, “to rust”, intransitive).

headline: Kakomu was kakumu in the Nara period, and likely shifted under the influence of 囲う (kakou).

sources.quote: Pronounced かくむ (kakumu) in the Nara period (奈(な)良(ら)時(じ)代(だい) (Nara jidai), 710–794 CE), it was alternately pronounced かこむ (kakomu) since the middle of the Heian period (平(へい)安(あん)時(じ)代(だい) (Heian jidai), 794–1185 CE). The shift to かこむ (kakomu) is likely due to influence from the verb 囲(かこ)う (kakou), of similar meaning.

An alternate pronunciation かごむ (kagomu), with the medial /k/ becoming voiced to /g/, was formerly widely used, as recorded in the 史記抄(しきしょう) (shikishō) written in the Muromachi period (室(むろ)町(まち)時(じ)代(だい) (Muromachi jidai), c. 1336–1573).

headline: Koeru is from Old Japanese 越ゆ (ko₁yu), from Proto-Japonic *koyai-.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 越ゆ (ko₁yu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern, from Proto-Japonic *koyai-.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

headline: Kagayaku was originally kakayaku; Samuel Martin suggests the kaka- element is mimetic.

sources.quote: Originally kakayaku. Samuel Martin suggests the initial kaka- element is a mimetic word. The -yaku element may be the verb-forming suffix やく (-yaku).
